**Summary.** Gene expression programs in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) carry prognostic information, but they are usually found by an unsupervised factorization that ignores survival. A Cox model is then fitted to the estimated scores, as if they were measured without error. This chapter develops survival-supervised Bayesian matrix factorization (SSBMF), which fits an empirical-Bayes factorization and a Cox model together. Program uncertainty is carried into the survival coefficients, and the number of programs is reduced from an over-specified starting rank by shrinkage. In five held-out PDAC cohorts the single-modality model's external concordance slightly exceeds that of an independently tuned two-step pipeline (mean 0.627 against 0.601), and its adverse (basal-like) and protective (classical) programs keep their direction out of sample. A multimodal extension to matched expression and methylation now selects the correct number of programs in simulation. On TCGA-to-ICGC data it matches the established model at the pre-specified rank, but its rank is not yet chosen reliably and methylation has not yet improved prediction. The remaining aims are to let survival inform the programs themselves, to make the number of programs data-driven on real multimodal data, and to determine what methylation contributes.

# Introduction {#sec-intro}

Section 1.3 of the literature review argues that PDAC expression contains prognostic tumor and stromal programs, with five-year survival of 13.7% [@SEER2026]. It also argues that the usual way of finding those programs has two weaknesses. Factorizing expression alone and testing survival afterward can miss a program that predicts survival but explains little expression variation, because cell-composition variation can dominate an expression-only fit (Section 1.3.2). Treating the estimated scores as fixed Cox covariates can attenuate their associations (Section 1.3.3). DeSurv lets survival guide discovery but reports penalized point estimates and tunes its rank and supervision strength by cross-validation [@Young2026]. Existing integration methods, such as MOFA [@Argelaguet2018] and iCluster [@Shen2009], combine cohorts or data types without survival supervision (Section 1.3.6).

This chapter takes up the approach the review closes on: a Bayesian factor model fitted together with a Cox model, which carries score uncertainty into the survival coefficients and estimates an effective number of programs by shrinkage (Sections 1.3.4–1.3.5). The review cautions that allowing survival to influence discovery is a possibility to demonstrate, not a property of the formulation. That caution matters here. In the current single-modality model survival does not yet shape the programs: the loading weight $\alpha_F$ is zero (@sec-single-model). Demonstrating supervised discovery is the first part of the remaining work (@sec-remaining). The review also notes that reconstruction-based rank criteria and survival-based criteria can disagree (Section 1.3.5); our multimodal results on real data give an example (@sec-res-mm-real).

## Contributions

This chapter combines empirical-Bayes matrix factorization [@Wang2021; @Willwerscheid2025] with a Cox proportional hazards model [@Cox1972; @Cox1975], fitted together by coordinate-ascent variational inference [@Blei2017]. Its first contribution is a supervised factor model whose risk score needs no fitted patient-level parameters: the Cox predictor projects each patient's expression onto the program loadings, so a new patient's risk is computed from their measurements alone, and posterior uncertainty in the survival coefficients is estimated within the model (@sec-single-model). The second is a shrinkage approach to the number of programs, in which an over-specified starting rank is reduced to an effective number of programs and programs that explain expression are separated from programs associated with survival. The third is external validation in five held-out PDAC cohorts across RNA-seq, microarray and proteomic platforms, against independently tuned two-step pipelines built with DeSurv's preprocessing and gene-selection rule. The fourth is a multimodal extension for matched gene expression and DNA methylation, with a parsimony framework that makes the final number of programs independent of the starting rank in simulation. The single-modality model and its validation are complete (Sections -@sec-res-external to -@sec-res-percohort); the multimodal model is implemented and has first results on real data (Sections -@sec-res-mm-sim and -@sec-res-mm-real); the work that remains is described in @sec-remaining.

# Methods

## Single-modality model {#sec-single-model}

For $n$ patients and $p$ genes, with log-scale expression standardized within each platform, the reconstruction model is $Y = LF^\top + E$ with $E_{ij}\sim N(0,\tau_j^{-1})$. $L$ ($n\times K$) holds patient program scores and $F$ ($p\times K$) gene loadings.^[Section 1.3.2 of the literature review writes $X\approx LF$ with $L$ the gene loadings; this chapter transposes that convention to match the EBMF software, so here $L$ holds patient scores.] Every entry of $L$ and $F$ has a point-exponential prior whose mixing proportion and rate are estimated by empirical Bayes for each program [@Willwerscheid2025].

Survival follows a Cox model with Breslow handling of ties [@Breslow1974] and linear predictor

$$
\eta_i=\sum_k (\hat z_F)_{ik}\,\tilde\beta_k,\qquad \hat Z_F = Y\,E[F]\,D^{-1},\quad D=\operatorname{diag}\lVert E[f_k]\rVert ,
$$

where $\hat Z_F$ is each patient's expression projected onto the unit-normalized loadings. The normalization only sets the units of $\tilde\beta$. The coefficients have Normal priors $\tilde\beta_k\sim N(0,s^2_{\beta_k})$ with empirical-Bayes variances. Within each iteration $\hat Z_F$ is held at its current value, so the single-modality coefficient update has no second-moment correction for uncertainty in $F$. The multimodal model adds one (@sec-mm-model).

The model is fitted by coordinate-ascent variational inference, using a second-order approximation of the Cox partial likelihood that is refreshed every iteration. Two weights are applied. A weight $\alpha=0.5$ tempers the Cox term in the coefficient update, and $\alpha_F=0$ keeps the Cox term out of the loading update. With $\alpha_F=0$, survival informs the coefficients but not the loadings, so the programs found are those that explain expression variance and are also associated with survival. Removing these weights is part of the remaining work (@sec-remaining).

The starting rank is chosen by a consensus of four criteria: the evidence lower bound (ELBO), BIC, a bi-cross-validated genomic log-likelihood and cross-validated concordance, followed by a one-standard-error rule [@Schwarz1978; @OwenPerry2009; @Breiman1984; @Hastie2009]. Programs in the over-specified fit are then classified as survival-active when the posterior mean $|\tilde\beta_k|$ exceeds $10^{-3}$, a cutoff set on the scale of the unit-normalized projection; as genomics-only when they are not survival-active but explain at least 1% of the expression variance; and otherwise as inactive.

Optional extensions allow a cohort-specific genomic offset, a stratified baseline hazard, and cohort-specific survival coefficients $\tilde\beta_k^{(c)}$ that share one estimated prior variance.

**Initialization and convergence.** Scores and loadings are initialized from a truncated singular value decomposition. Fitting stops when the relative change in the ELBO falls below $10^{-5}$, or after 100 iterations.

## Multimodal model {#sec-mm-model}

For matched expression $Y_1$ and methylation $Y_2$ on the same $n$ patients,

$$
Y_m = \mathbf 1\mu_m^\top + L F_m^\top + E_m,\qquad E_{mij}\sim N(0,\tau_{mj}^{-1}),\qquad m=1,2.
$$

$L\ge 0$ holds program activity, shared across modalities. $F_m$ describes how far each gene or CpG moves from its baseline $\mu_m$ when a program is active. The loading prior family is chosen per modality (point-exponential, point-Laplace or Normal), and its parameters are fitted for each modality–program pair, so a sparser prior can be estimated for the much larger CpG set. Cohorts and modalities enter differently: additional cohorts add rows of $L$ (patients), and additional modalities add rows of $F$ (features), each block with its own prior.

Survival follows a Cox model with $\boldsymbol\eta=(Y_1F_1+Y_2F_2)\,\beta$ and $\beta_k\sim N(0,s^2_{\beta_k})$. The coefficient update uses the projection's posterior second moment, $E[Z_{ik}^2]=\bar Z_{ik}^2+\sum_{m,j}y_{mij}^2\operatorname{Var}(f_{mjk})$, rather than its plug-in square. This propagates loading uncertainty into the survival coefficients, the correction for attenuation motivated in literature review Section 1.3.3. There are no tempering weights: the reconstruction and survival terms enter each loading update as a plain sum. Because rescaling a program's scores, loadings and coefficient together leaves the model unchanged, each program is rescaled after its update so that its projection has unit standard deviation. A program is called survival-active when $|E\beta_k|/\mathrm{SD}(\beta_k)\ge1.96$. The base update equations are in the project derivation document; the intercept, signed priors and pruning will be added to it.

**The parsimony framework** combines four changes to the original multimodal fitter: a per-feature intercept $\mu_m$, re-estimated every iteration; signed point-Laplace loadings; marginal-likelihood fits of each prior with the `ebnm` package, which allow a whole program to shrink to zero; and evidence-based pruning. At the end of fitting, a program is removed if the ELBO is no lower without it, with the other programs held fixed. The ELBO here is the expected reconstruction log-likelihood, plus the Cox partial log-likelihood at the posterior-mean predictor, minus the Kullback–Leibler divergence of each posterior from its prior. The model is then refitted from the remaining programs, and this repeats until no program can be removed. This follows the evidence-based check for dropping factors in flashier [@Willwerscheid2023].

Feature precisions $\tau_{mj}$ are estimated by maximum likelihood without regularization. Without the intercept, spare non-negative programs absorbed feature means and could fit single features exactly, so they were never removed. Adding the intercept removed this problem. The fitter is initialized from a truncated singular value decomposition of the stacked data. It stops when the relative change in both the fitted reconstruction and the risk score falls below $10^{-4}$, or after 500 iterations.

## Prediction in new cohorts

All screening and preprocessing choices are made on the training data. For the single-modality model, validation cohorts are log-transformed where needed, standardized within their own platform and restricted to the training genes, and the risk score is computed from the frozen loadings and coefficients. For the multimodal model, the validation data are restricted to the training features and scored with $\eta=(Y_1F_1+Y_2F_2)\beta$; the intercept enters only as a constant shift, which does not change concordance. In both cases the direction of the risk score is fixed from the training fit, before any validation outcome is seen.

## Comparators

The main comparator is a two-step pipeline: an unsupervised empirical-Bayes factorization followed by a Cox model on its scores. Its rank is chosen independently of the supervised model ($K=40$), and its Cox stage is penalized by LASSO with the penalty chosen by cross-validation. We also report a version with the rank matched to the supervised model ($K=7$) and the earlier unpenalized $K=20$ version. For the multimodal model we additionally report the same framework fitted to expression alone, the earlier version without the parsimony framework, two-step pipelines on each data configuration, and the established single-modality model scored on the same validation donors.

## Simulation designs

Two simulation studies were run (Table \ref{tab:sim-design}). The single-modality study uses two cohorts with shared and cohort-specific programs to study recovery, cohort attribution and the effect of the starting rank. The multimodal study uses matched expression and methylation to study recovery of the programs and of their number.

## Data and preprocessing

**Single-modality application.** The model is trained on TCGA-PAAD (144 patients) and CPTAC (129) [@Raphael2017; @Cao2021] and validated in five held-out cohorts: Dijk [@Dijk2020], Moffitt GEO array [@Moffitt2015], PACA-AU array and PACA-AU RNA-seq [@Bailey2016], and Puleo array [@Puleo2018]. Preprocessing is a log transformation where needed, standardization within each platform, and DeSurv's gene-selection rule: the top 3,000 genes per cohort by combined mean and variance rank, intersected across cohorts [@Young2026].

**Multimodal application.** The model is trained on TCGA-PAAD (144 patients, 75 deaths). It is validated on 50 primary-tumor PDAC donors from ICGC PACA-AU (30 deaths), with a sensitivity set of 67 donors (40 deaths) that adds IPMN with invasion and other histologies. Expression is on the log2 scale. Methylation beta-values are used on the 305,352 CpGs that pass both cohorts' sex-chromosome filters. Missing methylation values (0.07% in TCGA) are imputed by $k$-nearest neighbors within each cohort [@Troyanskaya2001]. Screening is done on the training cohort only: 3,000 genes by the DeSurv rule and the 10,000 most variable CpGs.

## Evaluation

Discrimination is measured by Harrell's concordance [@Harrell1982] in held-out cohorts, with percentile bootstrap intervals [@EfronTibshirani1993]. Differences between models use a paired bootstrap within each cohort (2,000 replicates), pooled by fixed-effect inverse-variance weighting. Because each risk score's direction is fixed from training, a model that fails in a cohort can show a concordance below 0.5. In simulation, a true program counts as recovered when the absolute correlation between true and estimated loadings is at least 0.7. Prognostic recall is the share of true prognostic programs whose matched program is survival-active with the correct sign; we also count false survival-active programs.

## Remaining work {#sec-remaining}

Two pieces of methodological work remain, each with an evaluation fixed in advance.

**Survival in the single-modality loadings.** The single-modality model sets the survival weight in the loading update to zero ($\alpha_F=0$), so its programs are those of an unsupervised factorization. Earlier attempts to include the survival term made the fit unstable. We will compare four ways of removing the weight while keeping the fit stable: rescaling each program after its update, as in the multimodal model; warm starts from the $\alpha_F=0$ solution; increasing the weight on the survival term gradually during fitting; and reordering the updates. The evaluation is a simulation with a planted low-variance prognostic program. A version counts as an improvement if it recovers the planted program (absolute loading correlation of at least 0.7) and classifies it as survival-active more often than the current model, without losing the high-variance programs, and if its pooled external concordance is no worse than the current model's (lower 95% limit of $\Delta C$ above $-0.02$). If no version meets these conditions, survival-guided discovery will be reported as not demonstrated for this model.

**Rank selection on real multimodal data and the contribution of methylation.** On TCGA the parsimony framework removes no programs, because $144\times13{,}000$ molecular values outweigh 75 survival events in the evidence used for pruning. We will add explicit weights to the ELBO, one balancing methylation against expression and one balancing survival against reconstruction, and evaluate them on a two-dimensional grid. We will also compare variance-based screening of CpGs with screening of CpGs linked to gene promoters. The weighting will be judged adequate if the final number of programs on real data varies by at most one across starting ranks 5 to 15, with recovery in simulation no worse than in the current results. Methylation will be judged to add value if the paired-bootstrap difference in external concordance against an expression-only fit excludes zero, or if it yields a prognostic program that the expression-only fit does not.

# Results

## The supervised model's external concordance slightly exceeds an independently tuned two-step pipeline {#sec-res-external}

The single-modality model, trained on TCGA-PAAD and CPTAC with a starting rank of 7, had a mean external concordance of 0.627 across the five held-out cohorts (Table \ref{tab:external}). The two-step pipeline with an independently chosen rank and a LASSO Cox stage reached 0.601. The pooled difference was $\Delta C=0.026$ (95% CI 0.0002 to 0.050). The supervised model was ahead in four of five cohorts, but no single cohort's difference was significant. With the two-step rank matched to the supervised model, the difference fell to 0.011 ($-0.013$ to 0.033) and was not significant; the earlier comparison with an unpenalized $K=20$ stage gave 0.042. Because $\alpha_F=0$, the factorization is unsupervised in both arms. The difference therefore reflects the priors, the shrunk and tempered survival stage and the rank, not supervised discovery of programs, and in practice the two approaches perform similarly.

```{=latex}
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
Validation cohort & $n$ & Supervised model & Two-step ($K=40$, LASSO) \\
\midrule
Dijk & 90 & 0.635 (0.555, 0.708) & 0.600 \\
Moffitt GEO array & 123 & 0.549 (0.467, 0.625) & 0.560 \\
PACA-AU array & 63 & 0.648 (0.553, 0.747) & 0.623 \\
PACA-AU RNA-seq & 52 & 0.657 (0.544, 0.772) & 0.603 \\
Puleo array & 288 & 0.645 (0.599, 0.688) & 0.618 \\
\midrule
Mean & & 0.627 & 0.601 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
```

In every held-out cohort the patients in the lowest third of predicted risk had the best survival (Figure \ref{fig:km-risk}). The log-rank test was significant in Puleo ($p<0.0001$), Dijk ($p=0.0005$) and PACA-AU RNA-seq ($p=0.021$). It was not significant in PACA-AU array ($p=0.075$) or Moffitt ($p=0.17$); Moffitt also had the lowest concordance.

## An over-specified fit retains two survival-associated programs and two expression programs

From a starting rank of 7, four programs were retained and three shrunk to zero (Figure \ref{fig:programs}). Program 7, associated with shorter survival, is enriched for *MET*, *ITGA3* and glycolytic genes, consistent with the basal-like program. Program 3, associated with longer survival, is enriched for epithelial (classical) genes. The other two retained programs explain expression without a survival association: one is stromal (collagens, *FAP*, *SPARC*, *CTHRC1*), and one combines immune genes (*IKZF1*, *IL10RA*) with quiescent-stroma genes (*COL14A1*, *TNXB*). Adverse or protective direction is read from each program's marginal survival association, because joint coefficients can change sign when correlated programs are fitted together.

```{=latex}
\begin{figure}[!htb]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.42\linewidth]{figures/single_programs_heatmap.png}
\caption{Gene weights of the four programs retained from a starting rank of 7 (top 12 genes per program, scaled to each program's largest weight).}\label{fig:programs}
\end{figure}
```

Both survival-associated programs kept their direction in data the model never saw (Figure \ref{fig:km-programs}). Across the 616 patients of the five held-out cohorts, patients in the top third of Program 7 activity had the shortest survival (cohort-stratified log-rank $p<0.0001$), and those in the top third of Program 3 activity the longest ($p=0.004$).

```{=latex}
\begin{figure}[!htb]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.8\linewidth]{figures/single_km_programs_external.png}
\caption{Overall survival by within-cohort tertile of Program 3 and Program 7 projection scores, pooled over the five held-out cohorts.}\label{fig:km-programs}
\end{figure}
```

## Under-specifying the starting rank merges true programs; over-specifying does not

In simulation, starting below the true rank (2–4) produced estimated programs that each correlated strongly with two true programs: 7 of 27 estimated programs were such merges. Starting at or above the true rank (6, 12 or 20) produced no merges (0 of 114). The concordance gain from joint fitting also depended on the starting rank (Figure \ref{fig:delta-c}). With shared and cohort-specific programs, the supervised model exceeded the two-step model at every starting rank of 3 or more, by up to 0.16 at a starting rank of 4 and by about 0.10 from 6 upward. With all programs shared it led only from a starting rank of 6, and with no shared programs the two models were within about 0.01. These results support over-specifying the starting rank and then shrinking.

```{=latex}
\begin{figure}[!htb]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.8\linewidth]{figures/single_delta_c_kinit.png}
\caption{Difference in held-out concordance between the supervised model and a two-step pipeline (unpenalized Cox stage) in simulation, by scenario and starting rank (mean $\pm$ 1 SE over 15 seeds; both models fitted to the same data).}\label{fig:delta-c}
\end{figure}
```

## The protective program's survival association is concentrated in one training cohort {#sec-res-percohort}

With cohort-specific survival coefficients, the adverse program's association was present in both training cohorts, while the protective program's came mainly from CPTAC (Figure \ref{fig:percohort}). In a simulation with a known truth, the model attributed the effect to the correct cohort in 15 of 20 seed–cohort cases at a starting rank of 6, and in 17 of 20 at 12. With training cohorts of 144 and 129 patients and no interval on the per-cohort coefficients, we interpret the CPTAC-specific effect cautiously. Cohort-specific coefficients did not change external concordance.

```{=latex}
\begin{figure}[!htb]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.7\linewidth]{figures/single_percohort_beta.png}
\caption{Cohort-specific survival coefficients of the seven programs (starting rank 7). Positive values indicate higher hazard.}\label{fig:percohort}
\end{figure}
```

## With the parsimony framework, the multimodal model's rank no longer depends on the starting rank {#sec-res-mm-sim}

Without the parsimony framework the multimodal model kept every starting program. With it, the final number of programs no longer depended on the starting rank (Figure \ref{fig:mm-pruning}). This was assessed in 486 fits: three scenarios, two noise levels, starting ranks 3–15 and three seeds. At moderate noise, where each true program explained about 10% of the variance, the final number stayed between 3.0 and 3.7 for every starting rank of 4 or more. The framework recovered essentially all true programs (2.96–3.00 of 3, against 2.74–2.78 without it) and converged in every run, against 7–37% of runs without it. Its held-out concordance was slightly higher (0.794–0.798 against 0.781–0.786), and it produced fewer false survival-active programs (0.59–0.67 against 0.70–0.82 per fit). At high noise, where each true program explained under 1% of the variance, the framework returned fewer than three programs, but its held-out concordance was much higher (0.79–0.81, against about 0.70). Neither version recovered the low-variance prognostic program at moderate noise.

```{=latex}
\begin{figure}[!htb]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.75\linewidth]{figures/multimodal_pruning_K_final.png}
\caption{Number of programs kept against the starting rank in simulation (true rank 3, dashed; $y=x$, dotted), with and without the parsimony framework; mean and range over three seeds.}\label{fig:mm-pruning}
\end{figure}
```

## On matched expression and methylation, the multimodal model reaches the established model's concordance; methylation adds little so far {#sec-res-mm-real}

Models were trained on TCGA (144 patients) and evaluated on 50 ICGC primary PDAC donors, all of whom are also in the PACA-AU RNA-seq validation cohort used above (Table \ref{tab:mm-external}). At the pre-specified starting rank of 7, which matches the single-modality model, the multimodal model reached a concordance of 0.685 (95% CI 0.579 to 0.779). The established single-modality model, trained on TCGA and CPTAC, also scored 0.685 on the same donors, so the multimodal model reached parity from a single training cohort. Fitted to expression alone, the same framework reached 0.676, so methylation added about 0.01, within the uncertainty. Without the parsimony framework, the multimodal model reached 0.453.

```{=latex}
\begin{table}[!htb]
\small\centering
\caption{External concordance (95\% bootstrap interval) on ICGC primary PDAC ($n=50$). Multimodal and two-step models were trained on TCGA with a starting rank of 7.}\label{tab:mm-external}
\begin{tabular}{>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{5.6cm}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{4.6cm}c}
\toprule
Model & Data & Concordance \\
\midrule
Multimodal, with the framework & Expression and methylation & 0.685 (0.579, 0.779) \\
Multimodal, with the framework & Expression only & 0.676 (0.569, 0.770) \\
Established single-modality model (TCGA and CPTAC) & Expression & 0.685 (0.576, 0.785) \\
Multimodal, without the framework & Expression and methylation & 0.453 (0.319, 0.599) \\
Two-step, factorization then Cox & Expression only & 0.525 (0.399, 0.651) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
```

The only survival-active program at this rank was the basal-like versus classical axis. It was prognostic in ICGC (hazard ratio 1.99 per standard deviation of its score, $p=0.0003$) and corresponds to the adverse single-modality program ($\lvert r\rvert=0.68$ on shared genes). The program corresponding to the protective single-modality program was retained but was not survival-active. Most of the fitted methylation signal went to a methylation-only program (59%) and an immune program (21%), neither of them prognostic. This suggests that the 10,000 most variable CpGs mainly reflect cell composition.

The real-data results depend strongly on the starting rank. Pruning removed no programs at any starting rank, so the starting rank also set the final number. Concordance across starting ranks 3–15 had a median of 0.57 (range 0.50–0.685). At a starting rank of 5 no program was survival-active, so the risk score was constant. At 15, eleven of fifteen programs were survival-active and concordance fell to 0.547. Most real-data fits reached the 500-iteration limit before meeting the convergence criterion, although their risk scores had stabilized.

\FloatBarrier

# Discussion

## Implications of findings

For a single modality, the supervised model gave external concordance slightly above that of an independently tuned two-step pipeline. The gain was significant only when pooled across cohorts and vanished when the pipeline was given the same rank. Its value lies less in prediction than in its outputs. It produced interpretable adverse and protective programs consistent with established PDAC subtypes, both kept their direction in held-out cohorts, and it reports posterior uncertainty for their survival associations. Starting from an over-specified rank and shrinking avoided merged programs. For multiple modalities, parsimony depended on modelling choices that matter less with one modality: a baseline intercept, signed loadings and evidence-based removal of programs. With these the multimodal model behaved as intended in simulation and matched the established model on real data, but methylation did not yet add discrimination.

## Limitations

The main limitation is that survival does not yet shape the programs. In the single-modality model the loading weight $\alpha_F$ is zero, so the discovery advantage motivated in @sec-intro has not been shown, and the programs found are high-variance programs that are also prognostic. In the multimodal model, reconstruction terms outnumber partial-likelihood terms by more than 10,000 to one. Survival changed the evidence for any TCGA program by less than 3 nats, against $10^4$–$10^5$ for reconstruction, so the choice of programs is driven by molecular variation. This is consistent with, though not shown to cause, the failure to recover low-variance prognostic programs and the absence of pruning on real data.

There are further limitations. The evidence bound used for pruning evaluates the partial likelihood at the posterior-mean predictor rather than taking its expectation. The matched multi-omic cohorts are small (50–67 validation donors) and ICGC includes mixed histologies. Feature screening for two modalities and the methylation scale (beta-values versus a variance-stabilizing transform) are not settled. Finally, the single-modality posterior intervals are tempered by $\alpha$ and conditional on the projection.

## Future directions and continuing work

This project is in progress. The remaining work (@sec-remaining) tests whether survival can inform the single-modality loadings without a tuning weight, and introduces modality and survival weights so that the multimodal model chooses its number of programs on real data and the contribution of methylation can be judged. Further extensions include a factor-level shrinkage prior on the number of programs [@BhattacharyaDunson2011; @GriffithsGhahramani2011], joint modelling of several cohorts and modalities, the full 305,352-CpG fit on the computing cluster, a direct comparison with DeSurv, and preparation of the manuscript for journal submission.
